s: Which of the following was a member of the seven-member Simon Commission?
x: Clement Attlee was one of the seven British members of the Simon Commission, which was chaired by Sir John Simon.

s: On which date did the Simon Commission arrive at Bombay?
x: The Simon Commission arrived at Bombay on 3 February 1928.

s: Which of the following did NOT join the boycott of the Simon Commission?
o: Jinnah's faction of the Muslim League
x: The Justice Party (like Shafi's League faction) did not join the boycott, while Jinnah's faction and the Hindu Mahasabha joined it.

s: Who coined the slogan 'Simon Go Back'?
x: Yusuf Meherally coined 'Simon Go Back' (APPSC GS 2018). Lajpat Rai led the Lahore protest, Prakasam the Madras protest, and S. Satyamurti headed the Andhra anti-Simon committee.

s: Which British Prime Minister's Conservative government appointed the Simon Commission (1927)?
x: The Conservative government of Stanley Baldwin appointed the Simon Commission on 8 November 1927, two years early, to review the 1919 Act.

s: Who presided over the Madras Congress session (December 1927) that resolved to boycott the Simon Commission 'at every stage and in every form'?
x: The Madras Congress of December 1927 under M.A. Ansari decided to boycott the Simon Commission.

s: What was the official name of the Simon Commission?
x: The Simon Commission was officially the Indian Statutory Commission; it was also called the 'White Commission'.

s: The Simon Commission was appointed in November 1927 by the government of which British Prime Minister?
x: The Conservative government of Stanley Baldwin appointed it to study the working of the 1919 Act; MacDonald was PM during the Round Table Conferences.

s: How many members did the Simon Commission have?
x: It had seven members, all British, headed by Sir John Simon.

s:
Consider the following statements about the Simon Commission:
1. It was headed by Sir John Simon of the Liberal Party.
2. Clement Attlee was one of its members.
3. It had one Indian member.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: Simon (Liberal) headed it and Attlee was a member; it had no Indian member, which is why it was boycotted.

s: When did the Simon Commission arrive at Bombay?
x: It arrived on 3 February 1928; 26 February 1928 was the Madras protest and 11 October 1928 began its second visit.

s: When was the Gandhi-Irwin Pact signed?
x: The Gandhi-Irwin Pact was signed in March 1931; 'March 1930' is a known trap (March 1930 was the start of the Dandi March). December 1929 was the Lahore session and August 1932 the Communal Award.

s: The three Round Table Conferences in London were held under which British Prime Minister?
x: All three Round Table Conferences were held in London under Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald to discuss the Simon Report and a federal constitution.

s: What did Mahatma Gandhi do after returning from the Second Round Table Conference?
o: attended the Third Round Table Conference
resumed the Civil Disobedience Movement and was jailed in Yerwada
x: After the Second Conference, Gandhi resumed the Civil Disobedience Movement and was imprisoned in Yerwada; the Communal Award followed in August 1932.

s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: First Round Table Conference — Congress represented by Gandhi
Second Round Table Conference — Gandhi as sole INC representative
Third Round Table Conference — attended by Congress under Jawaharlal Nehru
First Round Table Conference — held after the Gandhi-Irwin Pact
x: Gandhi attended the Second Round Table Conference as the sole representative of the Indian National Congress. Congress boycotted the First and Third Conferences.

s: How many delegates attended the Third Round Table Conference?
x: Only 46 delegates attended the Third RTC (Nov-Dec 1932), from which Congress and Jinnah were absent.

s: The White Paper that led to the Government of India Act, 1935 followed which Round Table Conference?
x: The Third RTC (1932) produced the White Paper leading to the 1935 Act.

s: In which year was the Third Round Table Conference held?
x: The Third Round Table Conference met in London from 17 November to 24 December 1932, without the Congress.

s: In which city were the three Round Table Conferences held?
x: All three Round Table Conferences (1930-32) were held in London under Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald.

s: What was the main aim of the Round Table Conferences held in London during 1930-32?
o: To discuss the Simon report and a federal constitution for India
To plan the partition of India
To review the working of the Rowlatt Act
To set up a Constituent Assembly for India
x: The Round Table Conferences were called to discuss the Simon report and a federal constitution for India.

s: On which date was the Gandhi-Irwin Pact signed?
x: It was signed on 5 March 1931, after which Gandhi agreed to attend the Second RTC.

s: The Nehru Report was primarily prepared in response to which of the following?
o: Lord Birkenhead's challenge to Indians to frame a constitution
The demand for a separate Muslim homeland
The failure of the Cripps Mission
x: The Nehru Report was prepared in reply to Secretary of State Lord Birkenhead's challenge to Indians to frame their own constitution.

s: Who chaired the Nehru Report committee of the All Parties Conference (1928)?
x: Motilal Nehru chaired the committee; Jawaharlal Nehru was its secretary.

s: What did the All Parties Muslim Conference held at Delhi (from 31 December 1928) under the Aga Khan do?
o: drafted the Government of India Act, 1935
resolved to boycott the Simon Commission at every stage
accepted the Nehru Report without modification
x: The All Parties Muslim Conference met at Delhi from 31 December 1928 to 1 January 1929 under the Aga Khan. It rejected the Nehru Report and demanded separate electorates.

s: Which of the following pairs relating to the reaction to the Nehru Report is correctly matched?
o: Rejection of the Nehru Report – Muslim League
One-year ultimatum to Britain – Muslim League
x: The Muslim League rejected the Nehru Report. Nehru and Bose demanded complete independence, Congress gave Britain a one-year ultimatum, and complete independence was declared at Lahore in 1929.

s: The challenge issued by Birkenhead in 1927, which led to the formation of the committee for the Nehru Report, was that Indians
o: could not organise a boycott of the Simon Commission
could not agree on a constitutional scheme
x: Birkenhead challenged Indians to prepare an agreed constitutional scheme, leading to the All Parties Conference and the Nehru Report committee.

s: When was the Nehru Report, drafted by a committee chaired by Motilal Nehru, published?
x: The Nehru Report came out in August 1928; 1929 is a known trap.

s: Who served as secretary of the committee that drafted the Nehru Report?
x: Jawaharlal Nehru was the secretary; the report recommended a Supreme Court and proposed ending dyarchy.

s: Which of the following was NOT a recommendation of the Nehru Report?
o: Universal adult suffrage and fundamental rights
Separate electorates as the permanent basis of representation
A federal structure with a bicameral central legislature
x: The Nehru Report recommended joint electorates with reserved seats for minorities, not separate electorates as a permanent arrangement.

s: Who presided over the All Parties Conference that set up the Nehru Report committee?
x: Ansari presided the All Parties Conference; Motilal Nehru chaired the drafting committee.

s: The Nehru Report demanded which status for India?
x: It sought dominion status; Jawaharlal Nehru and Bose wanted complete independence.

s:
Consider the following statements about the Nehru Report:
1. It recommended joint electorates with reserved seats for minorities.
2. It recommended a Supreme Court.
3. It was submitted at Lucknow in August 1928.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: All three are correct: joint electorates with reserved seats, a bicameral centre with a Supreme Court, and submission at Lucknow on 28 August 1928.

s: After the Nehru Report, the Congress ultimatum led to the Purna Swaraj resolution at which session?
x: The one-year ultimatum led to Purna Swaraj at Lahore in December 1929; Jinnah's amendments had failed at Calcutta in 1928.

s: At which convention did Jinnah's amendments to the Nehru Report fail in December 1928?
x: Jinnah's amendments were rejected at the Calcutta All Parties Convention (December 1928), and the League rejected the report.

s: Who among the following was a member of the Nehru Report committee (1928)?
x: Members included Tej Bahadur Sapru, Ali Imam, Subhas Chandra Bose and M.S. Aney; Motilal Nehru was chairman.

s: Under whose chairmanship did the committee of the All Parties Conference prepare the Nehru Report of 1928?
x: The committee that prepared the Nehru Report was chaired by Motilal Nehru. Jawaharlal Nehru served as its secretary.

s: What did the Nehru Report (1928) ask for India?
x: The Nehru Report proposed a constitution based on Dominion Status.

s: Who was the secretary of the committee that prepared the Nehru Report (1928)?
x: Motilal Nehru was chairman and Jawaharlal Nehru was secretary.

s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched in relation to participation in all three Round Table Conferences?
o: B.R. Ambedkar and Tej Bahadur Sapru
x: B.R. Ambedkar and Tej Bahadur Sapru attended all three Round Table Conferences.

s:
Consider the following statements about the Round Table Conferences:
1. M.A. Jinnah was absent from the Third Round Table Conference.
2. B.R. Ambedkar attended all three Round Table Conferences.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: Both are correct: Jinnah, like the Congress, was absent from the Third RTC, while Ambedkar and Sapru attended all three.

s: Besides Gandhi, which of the following attended the Second Round Table Conference (1931)?
o: Jawaharlal Nehru and Subhas Chandra Bose
x: Sarojini Naidu and Muhammad Iqbal attended the Second RTC (Sept-Dec 1931), where Gandhi was the sole INC representative (APPSC G2 2005). Nehru, Bose, Patel and Azad did not attend; Motilal Nehru and C.R. Das had died before 1931.

s: Tanguturi Prakasam acquired the title 'Andhra Kesari' in connection with which incident?
o: Baring his chest before the police during the anti-Simon Commission protest at Madras
Leading the Home Rule League in Andhra
Leading the boycott of the Rowlatt Act in Guntur
x: Tanguturi Prakasam bared his chest before the police during the anti-Simon Commission protest at Madras and became known as Andhra Kesari.

s: Which pair of anti-Simon Commission protest centre and leader is INCORRECTLY matched?
o: Tenali and Guntur – G.V. Unnayya Sastri
x: The Lucknow protest was led by Jawaharlal Nehru and G.B. Pant; G.V. Unnayya Sastri led the protests at Tenali and Guntur.

s: Whom did Bhagat Singh and Rajguru shoot in December 1928 to avenge the death of Lala Lajpat Rai?
x: Saunders was shot in December 1928 in revenge for Lajpat Rai's death after the Lahore lathi charge.

s: Who led the anti-Simon Commission protest at Lucknow?
x: At Lucknow the protest was led by Jawaharlal Nehru and G.B. Pant.

s: Where was Lala Lajpat Rai fatally injured in a lathi charge while leading the anti-Simon protest?
x: Lajpat Rai led the 1928 Lahore protest and died of the lathi-charge injuries.

s: Who presided over the first session of the All India Trade Union Congress (AITUC) in 1920?
x: Lala Lajpat Rai, who later died after the anti-Simon lathi charge, presided over AITUC's first session (1920).

s: The leader who died of injuries from a lathi charge during the anti-Simon protest at Lahore had earlier presided over the first session of which body?
x: Lala Lajpat Rai had presided over the first session of AITUC in 1920.

s: What did Tanguturi Prakasam do to earn the title 'Andhra Kesari'?
o: drafted the Nehru Report in Andhra
bared his chest and dared the police to shoot during the Simon protest
organised the first Round Table Conference
led the boycott resolution at the Madras Congress session
x: During the Simon protest, Prakasam bared his chest and challenged the police to shoot, earning the title ‘Andhra Kesari’.

s: Who was killed in the police firing during the Simon Commission protest in Madras?
x: Police firing during the Madras protest killed Parthasarathi.

s: Where were black flags shown against the Simon Commission in Andhra?
x: Black flags were shown at Guntur and Ongole. G. V. Unnayya Sastri led protests at Tenali and Guntur.

s: Who was the President of the Andhra Boycott Committee against the Simon Commission?
x: S. Satyamurthy presided the Andhra Boycott Committee; Unnayya Sastri led Tenali-Guntur and Kaleswara Rao was Vijayawada's municipal chairman.

s: Which pair relating to the Simon boycott in Andhra is correctly matched?
o: Tenali and Guntur – Ayyadevara Kaleswara Rao
x: Kaleswara Rao, Vijayawada municipal chairman, issued a cover reading only 'Simon Go Back'; Unnayya Sastri led Tenali and Guntur.

s: In which document was the term 'Scheduled Castes' first used?
x: The term 'Scheduled Castes' was first used in the Simon Commission Report.

s: Which group lobbied the Simon Commission and saw its provincial demand supported in the report?
x: The Oriyas lobbied the Simon Commission and the report supported the creation of Orissa; the Andhras boycotted it and their demand was ignored.

s: What did the Simon Commission report recommend on electorates?
x: The report recommended continuing separate communal electorates, along with abolition of dyarchy and provincial autonomy.

s: The Simon Commission report recommended the creation of which new province?
x: The report recommended creating Orissa as a province (and separating Sindh and Burma), but ignored Andhra's demand for a separate province.

s: Which demand was fuelled by the Simon Commission's neglect of Andhra's demand and Prakasam's 'Andhra Kesari' moment?
o: restoration of dyarchy in the provinces
x: The Simon Commission's neglect of Andhra's demand and Prakasam's role fuelled the demand for a separate Andhra Province.

s: The Simon Commission report recommended separating which territory from India?
x: It proposed separating Burma from India and Sindh from Bombay.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the Simon Commission report?
o: It recommended abolishing dyarchy in the provinces
It recommended keeping separate communal electorates
It became the base of the Government of India Act, 1935
It recommended a separate Andhra province
x: The report created Orissa but ignored Andhra's demand; the other statements are correct.

s: In which year was the report of the Simon Commission published?
x: The Simon Commission report came out in two volumes in June 1930.

s: Which one of the following is NOT correctly matched?
o: Butler Committee — relations of princely states with the Paramount Power
Simon Commission — review of the Government of India Act, 1919
Butler Committee — chaired by Lord Irwin
x: The Butler Committee was associated with Harcourt Butler, not Lord Irwin. Its purpose was to examine relations between princely states and the Paramount Power.

s: Who issued the Deepavali Declaration of 1929?
x: Lord Irwin issued the Deepavali Declaration in 1929, promising a Round Table Conference after the Simon Commission report.

s: Besides declaring dominion status as India's goal, what did the Deepavali Declaration of 1929 promise?
o: A Round Table Conference after the Simon report
x: Irwin's declaration of 31 October 1929 promised a Round Table Conference after the Simon report.

s: Who headed the Butler Committee of 1927?
x: Sir Harcourt Butler headed it, not Irwin; its 1929 report upheld paramountcy.

s: Jinnah's Fourteen Points of 1929 were formulated as the Muslim League's response to which document?
x: Jinnah's Fourteen Points were the Muslim League's answer to the Nehru Report.

s: Which one of the following combinations correctly represents important features of Jinnah's Fourteen Points?
o: Unitary constitution, joint electorates and abolition of provincial autonomy
Federal constitution, residuary powers to provinces and separate electorates
Dominion status, nominated legislatures and universal adult franchise
Presidential government, one-third provincial seats and communal veto at all levels
x: Jinnah's Fourteen Points demanded a federal constitution with residuary powers to the provinces and separate electorates.

s: In which year were Jinnah's Fourteen Points formulated?
x: Jinnah's Fourteen Points came in 1929, after the Nehru Report (1928) and before the Gandhi-Irwin Pact (March 1931).

s: At which session were Jinnah's Fourteen Points presented in March 1929?
o: Indian National Congress session at Lahore
Second Round Table Conference at London
x: Jinnah presented the Fourteen Points in March 1929 at the Muslim League session in Delhi.

s: What did the Delhi Proposals support on the question of electorates?
x: The Delhi Proposals supported joint electorates subject to safeguards such as the separation of Sindh and one-third Muslim representation at the Centre.

s: Jinnah's Fourteen Points demanded what share of Muslim representation at the Centre?
x: Jinnah's Fourteen Points demanded one-third Muslim representation at the Centre, along with provincial residuary powers, separate electorates and safeguards for Muslim-majority provinces.

s: The Delhi Proposals of March 1927 demanded the separation of which region from Bombay?
x: The Delhi Proposals asked for a separate Sindh, one-third central seats and reforms in NWFP and Baluchistan.

s: In whom did Jinnah's Fourteen Points want residuary powers vested?
x: The Fourteen Points sought a federal constitution with residuary powers to the provinces.

s: Which Act was the longest British Act of Parliament up to its time?
x: The Government of India Act, 1935, passed in August 1935, was the longest British Act to that time.

s: Which Act, with changes, served as the working constitution of India until 26 January 1950?
x: Until the Constitution came into force on 26 January 1950, India was governed by the Government of India Act, 1935, as adapted.

s: The Government of India Act, 1935 further extended the system of separate electorates to include which of the following groups?
o: Workers, soldiers and civil servants only
x: The separate electorate system was extended further to depressed classes, women and labour.

s: On which date did provincial autonomy under the Government of India Act, 1935 come into force?
x: Provincial autonomy began on 1 April 1937, with Governors keeping reserve powers.

s: Which of the following provisions of the Government of India Act, 1935 was NOT implemented?
o: Abolition of the Council of India
x: The Federation never came into force because too few princes acceded; the others were implemented.

s: When was the Federal Court under the Government of India Act, 1935 set up at Delhi?
x: The Federal Court was established at Delhi in October 1937.

s:
Consider the following statements about the Government of India Act, 1935:
1. Dyarchy at the Centre never came into force.
2. The Council of India advising the Secretary of State was abolished.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: Both are correct: central dyarchy was part of the unrealised federal scheme, and the Council of India was abolished.

s: Which provision of the Government of India Act, 1935 served as a model for the Directive Principles of State Policy?
x: The Instrument of Instructions under the Government of India Act, 1935 served as the model for the Directive Principles of State Policy.

s: How many subjects did the Federal List contain under the Government of India Act, 1935?
x: The Federal List had 59 subjects, the Provincial List 54 and the Concurrent List 36.

s: The idea behind Section 63 of the Government of India Act, 1935, on the Governor's address to the provincial legislature, is carried in which Article of the Constitution of India?
x: Article 175 (the Governor's address) carries the idea of Section 63 of the 1935 Act. Today the speech reflects the elected ministry's policy rather than the Governor's own discretion.

s: How many subjects did the Provincial List contain under the Government of India Act, 1935?
x: The lists had 59 (Federal), 54 (Provincial) and 36 (Concurrent) subjects.

s: How many subjects did the Concurrent List under the Government of India Act, 1935 contain?
x: The Concurrent List had 36 subjects; Federal 59 and Provincial 54.

s: Which one of the following sets contains only features borrowed from the Government of India Act, 1935?
o: Concurrent List, joint sitting and freedom of trade
Fundamental Rights, judicial review, impeachment and Vice-President
Federal scheme, office of Governor, judiciary and Public Service Commissions
Fundamental Duties, Five-Year Plans and ideals of justice
x: The Government of India Act, 1935 contributed the federal scheme, office of Governor, judiciary and Public Service Commissions, among other administrative features.

s: Which Act is correctly associated with the introduction of dyarchy in the provinces, bicameralism at the Centre and direct elections?
x: These three features were introduced by the Government of India Act, 1919, also known as the Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms.

s: Which of the following was borrowed into the Constitution from the Government of India Act, 1935?
o: Bicameralism and direct elections at the Centre
Public Service Commissions and the office of Governor
x: The 1935 Act gave the federal scheme, office of Governor, judiciary, PSCs and emergency provisions.

s: How many sections and schedules did the Government of India Act, 1935, the longest British Act on India, contain?
x: The Act contained 321 sections and 10 schedules; some references describe it as having 14 parts and 321 articles.

s: When did provincial autonomy under the Government of India Act, 1935 begin?
x: Provincial autonomy, which replaced dyarchy in the provinces, began in April 1937.

s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Federal Public Service Commission — 1935 Act — Calcutta, 1937
Provincial Public Service Commissions — 1909 Act — Delhi, 1910
x: The Federal Court was established at Delhi in 1937 under the Government of India Act, 1935. The Act also provided for a Federal PSC and Provincial PSCs.

s: In which year was the Federal Court under the Government of India Act, 1935 set up at Delhi?
x: The Federal Court began at Delhi in 1937.

s: On whose recommendation was the Reserve Bank of India set up?
x: The RBI Act, 1934 followed the Hilton Young Commission (1926); the RBI started on 1 April 1935.

s:
Consider the following statements about the Reserve Bank of India:
1. It started functioning on 1 April 1935.
2. It was nationalised on 1 January 1949.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: The RBI started on 1 April 1935 under the RBI Act, 1934 and was nationalised on 1 January 1949.

s: Which function of the Governor did Section 63 of the Government of India Act, 1935 deal with?
x: Section 63 enabled the Governor to address the provincial legislature in his discretion.

s: The Instrument of Instructions in the Government of India Act, 1935 became which part of the Constitution?
x: The Instrument of Instructions became the Directive Principles (APPSC 2023), not Fundamental Rights.

s: Which pair (feature of the 1935 Act – counterpart in the Constitution) is INCORRECTLY matched?
o: Federal scheme and PSCs – Union-State structure and UPSC/State PSCs
x: The Instrument of Instructions corresponds to the Directive Principles of State Policy, not the Fundamental Rights.

s: When were the provincial elections under the Government of India Act, 1935 held?
x: Elections were held in winter 1936-37 in 11 provinces; ministries followed in 1937.

s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Bengal — Unionist Party ministry under Sikandar Hayat Khan
Bengal — Coalition led by Fazlul Huq's Krishak Praja Party
x: In Bengal, Fazlul Huq's Krishak Praja Party formed a coalition. Punjab was associated with the Unionist Party under Sikandar Hayat Khan, while Sindh had a coalition under Allah Baksh.

s: How did the Muslim League fare in the 1937 provincial elections?
o: It did poorly even in Muslim seats
It won a clear majority in Bengal
It formed ministries in all Muslim-majority provinces
x: The League performed poorly even in Muslim seats, after which it alleged 'Hindu Raj' and launched mass-contact campaigns.

s: Under whom was the Unionist Party ministry formed in Punjab after the 1937 elections?
x: Sikandar Hayat Khan's Unionist Party formed the Punjab ministry; there was no Congress ministry there.

s: Under whom was the coalition ministry formed in Sindh after the 1937 elections?
x: Sindh had a coalition under Allah Baksh.

s: Who led the coalition ministry in Bengal after the 1937 elections?
x: Congress lacked an absolute majority in Bengal; Fazlul Huq's Krishak Praja Party led the coalition.

s: In how many of the eleven provinces did the Congress form ministries after the 1937 elections?
x: Congress formed ministries in eight of the eleven provinces, including Bombay, Madras, Central Provinces, Orissa, Bihar, UP, NWFP and Assam.

s: What was 'Begar', abolished by the Congress ministries of 1937-39?
x: Begar was forced labour, not a salt tax; the Congress ministries abolished it.

s: How did Mahatma Gandhi advise the Congress ministries to hold office?
o: firmly and permanently as a constitutional right
only until the completion of the war
lightly, not tightly, as a crown of thorns
x: Gandhi advised the ministers to hold office “lightly, not tightly”, describing office as a “crown of thorns”.

s: In how many provinces did the Congress win a clear majority on its own in 1937?
x: It won a clear majority in five (Madras, UP, CP, Bihar, Orissa) but formed ministries in eight.

s: Which labour law was passed during the Congress ministries of 1937-39?
x: The Congress ministries passed the Industrial Disputes Act (1938) and protected trade-union rights.

s: Which of the following was NOT a measure of the Congress ministries of 1937-39?
o: Introduction of separate electorates for labour
x: Separate electorates for labour came from the 1935 Act itself; the ministries released prisoners, passed tenancy laws and abolished begar.

s: Besides the six provinces of July 1937, in which two provinces did the Congress later form ministries?
x: After Bombay, Madras, CP, Orissa, Bihar and UP, the Congress later formed ministries in NWFP and Assam, making 8 of 11.

s: Which party formed the ministry in the Madras Presidency after the 1937 elections?
x: The Congress formed the Madras ministry, while the Justice Party was almost wiped out and the People's Party lost all its seats.

s: Which party, led by the Pithapuram Zamindar, lost all its seats in the 1937 Madras elections?
x: In Madras the Justice Party was almost wiped out and the Pithapuram Zamindar's People's Party lost all seats.

s: At whose house was the Sri Bagh Pact (November 1937) concluded?
x: The pact, which sought to close the Coastal-Rayalaseema rift, was concluded at Kasinathuni Nageswara Rao's house 'Sreerbagh', not Prakasam's.

s: In the 1937 Madras Congress ministry and legislature, which pair is correctly matched?
x: V.V. Giri held Labour and Industries; Prakasam held Revenue, Bezawada Gopala Reddy Local Self-Government, and Bulusu Sambamurthy was Speaker.

s: In the 1937 Madras Congress ministry, Bezawada Gopala Reddy held which portfolio?
x: Bezawada Gopala Reddy held Local Self-Government; Prakasam was Revenue and V.V. Giri Labour and Industries.

s: Who led the agitation against Rajaji's introduction of Hindi in Madras schools in 1937?
x: Periyar led the anti-Hindi agitation of 1937, and the measure was withdrawn.

s: Which Andhra leader was Minister for Labour and Industries in the 1937 Madras ministry?
x: V.V. Giri held Labour and Industries; Sambamurthy was Speaker.

s: Which of the following was concluded in November 1937 to end the split between Coastal Andhra and Rayalaseema?
x: The Sri Bagh Pact was made in November 1937 at Kasinathuni Nageswara Rao's house to end the Coastal-Rayalaseema split.

s: Who was the Speaker of the Madras Legislative Assembly after the 1937 elections?
x: Bulusu Sambamurthy became Speaker; Prakasam was Revenue Minister.

s: Which portfolio did Tanguturi Prakasam hold in the Rajagopalachari ministry of 1937?
x: Prakasam was Revenue Minister in the 1937 Madras Congress ministry.

s: After the 1937 provincial elections, who became the Congress Premier of Madras?
x: Rajaji headed Madras's first Congress ministry after the 1937 elections under the 1935 Act.

s: Which Congress session of 1936 decided to contest the elections under the Government of India Act, 1935?
x:
Many notes: Faizpur (Dec 1936) = decided to contest. Strictly, Lucknow (April 1936) took that decision first and Faizpur reaffirmed it (PMF Part 5 p.20; Spectrum pdf p.441).
The Lucknow session (April 1936) already resolved to contest the elections on a manifesto, keeping office acceptance pending; Faizpur (Dec 1936) only reaffirmed it. Haripura and Tripuri are 1938-39.

s: Who first raised the demand for a Constituent Assembly in 1934?
x: M.N. Roy first raised the Constituent Assembly demand in 1934; the Congress adopted it officially in 1935.

s: Who described the Government of India Act, 1935 as “thoroughly rotten, fundamentally bad and totally unacceptable”?
x: Muhammad Ali Jinnah used the description “thoroughly rotten, fundamentally bad and totally unacceptable” for the Act.

s: Who described the Government of India Act, 1935 as a 'Charter of Slavery' and as 'a machine with strong brakes but no engine'?
x: Jawaharlal Nehru used both descriptions. Jinnah called the Act 'thoroughly rotten, fundamentally bad and totally unacceptable'; M.N. Roy first raised the Constituent Assembly demand (1934).

s: In 1934, the demand for a Constituent Assembly was first raised by M.N. Roy. In which year did the Congress adopt it officially?
x: M.N. Roy raised it in 1934 and the Congress adopted it officially in 1935.

s: Which Congress session of 1936, presided over by Jawaharlal Nehru, rejected the Government of India Act, 1935?
x: The Lucknow session (1936, Nehru) rejected the Act; the Faizpur session (1936) decided to contest the elections.

s: Why did the Congress ministries resign in October-November 1939?
o: The Muslim League withdrew support from all provincial ministries.
India was involved in the Second World War without the consent of Indian leaders.
The British abolished provincial legislatures without consultation.
The Federal Court rejected provincial autonomy.
x: The Congress ministries resigned in protest against India being dragged into the Second World War without Indian consent.

s: On which date did the Muslim League observe the 'Day of Deliverance' after the Congress ministries resigned?
x: The League observed 22 December 1939 as the Day of Deliverance after the Congress ministries resigned in October-November 1939.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the events of 1939-40?
o: Linlithgow declared India a party to the Second World War in September 1939
The Congress ministries resigned in October-November 1939
The Muslim League observed Deliverance Day on 22 December 1939
The Lahore Resolution was adopted before the Congress ministries resigned
x: The Lahore Resolution was adopted on 23 March 1940, after the ministries resigned in October-November 1939; the other three are correct.

s: On which date did Lord Linlithgow declare India at war with Germany without consulting Indian leaders?
x: The declaration on 3 September 1939 led the Congress ministries to resign in Oct-Nov 1939.

s: The Congress ministries resigned in 1939 in protest against which act of Viceroy Lord Linlithgow?
o: Declaring India at war with Germany without consulting Indian leaders
x: On 3 September 1939 Linlithgow declared India at war with Germany without consulting Indian leaders, so the Congress ministries resigned in October-November 1939.

s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
x: The Lahore Resolution, demanding independent states for Muslims, was passed in 1940. Direct Action Day was in 1946 (not 1940), the Lahore Resolution was not in 1946, and Iqbal's Allahabad address was in 1930 (1933 is when Rahmat Ali coined 'Pakistan').

s: What did the Lahore (Pakistan) Resolution of 1940 demand?
x: The Lahore Resolution of 1940 demanded separate independent states for Muslims, hence the name Pakistan Resolution.

s: Who moved the Lahore Resolution at the Muslim League session of March 1940?
x: A.K. Fazlul Haq, Premier of Bengal, moved the Lahore Resolution in 1940; Jinnah presided over the session. The Aga Khan was the League's first President and Liaquat Ali Khan became Pakistan's first Prime Minister.

s: Who drafted the Lahore Resolution of 1940?
x: Sikandar Hayat Khan drafted it; Fazlul Haq moved it, Khaliquzzaman approved it and Jinnah presided.

s: Who became the first Prime Minister of Pakistan?
x: Liaquat Ali Khan was Pakistan's first Prime Minister.

s: Who moved the Lahore Resolution on 23 March 1940?
x: A.K. Fazlul Huq moved the Lahore (Pakistan) Resolution; Sikandar Hayat Khan drafted it and Jinnah presided.

s: Who presided over the Lahore session of the Muslim League in March 1940?
x: Jinnah presided; Sikandar Hayat Khan drafted and Fazlul Huq moved the resolution.

s: In reply to the Lahore Resolution, Periyar demanded Dravidistan at which conference in 1940?
x: Periyar demanded Dravidistan at the Erode Conference, 1940.

s: What did the Lahore Resolution demand?
o: Independent states for Muslims in Muslim-majority areas
A single federation with weak Centre
x: It demanded independent states for Muslims in Muslim-majority areas and was soon called the Pakistan Resolution.

s: Which resolution was drafted by Sikandar Hayat Khan, the Unionist Premier of Punjab?
x: Sikandar Hayat Khan drafted the Lahore Resolution of 1940; Fazlul Huq moved it and Jinnah presided over the session.

s: On which date did the Muslim League observe Direct Action Day?
x: Direct Action Day was observed on 16 August 1946, leading to large riots in Calcutta.

s: Who proposed the idea of a Muslim state in the North-West of India in the Allahabad Address of 1930?
x: Muhammad Iqbal proposed the idea of a Muslim state in the North-West in his Allahabad Address of 1930.

s: What was the title of the pamphlet in which Chaudhry Rahmat Ali coined the name 'PAKISTAN' in 1933?
x: Chaudhry Rahmat Ali coined the name “PAKISTAN” in 1933 in the pamphlet Now or Never.

s: In which of the following was the Two-Nation Theory formally set out?
x: The Lahore Resolution of 1940 formally set out the Two-Nation Theory.

s: Who among the following was associated with the early advocacy of keeping Muslims away from the Indian National Congress in 1887?
x: In 1887-88 Lord Dufferin used Sayyid Ahmad Khan as an anti-Congress front, along with Raja Shiva Prasad of Benares and the Raja of Bhinga; the United Indian Patriotic Association followed in 1888.

s: With which proposal is the 1930 Allahabad address of Muhammad Iqbal associated?
o: Immediate withdrawal of the British from India
A federation of all princely states
A consolidated Muslim state in north-western India
x: In his 1930 Allahabad address, Iqbal advocated a consolidated Muslim state in the north-western region.

s: The Shimla Deputation of 1906 is associated with which of the following developments?
o: Acceptance of complete independence by the Congress
Demand for separate electorates and the founding of the Muslim League
Replacement of reserved seats by joint electorates
x: The 1906 Shimla Deputation, led by Aga Khan, demanded separate electorates, and the Muslim League was founded in the same year.

s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
x: The Lahore Resolution was in 1940; the Nehru Report belongs to 1928–29, Iqbal's Allahabad Address to 1930 and Rahmat Ali's Now or Never to 1933.

s: Who coined the word 'Pakistan' in 1933?
x: Chaudhry Rahmat Ali coined the word 'Pakistan' in 1933.

s: Along with whom did Lord Dufferin use Sayyid Ahmad Khan as an anti-Congress front?
x: Sayyid Ahmad Khan was used with Raja Shiva Prasad of Benares and the Raja of Bhinga in 1887-88.

s: In which year was the United Indian Patriotic Association formed?
x: It was formed in 1888 as an anti-Congress front.

s: Who led the Shimla Deputation of 1906 that demanded separate electorates for Muslims?
x: The Shimla Deputation (1906) under the Aga Khan demanded separate electorates; the Muslim League was founded the same year.

s: Which of the following combinations correctly represents the elements used in the acronym 'Pakistan'?
o: Punjab, Afghan, Kashmir, Sindh and Baluchistan
Punjab, Assam, Kashmir, Sindh and Bengal
Peshawar, Afghan, Karachi, Sindh and Bengal
Punjab, Afghanistan, Khyber, Sindh and Bengal
x: The acronym was explained through Punjab, Afghan or NWFP, Kashmir, Sindh and Baluchistan.

s: At which university was Chaudhry Rahmat Ali a student when he coined the word 'Pakistan'?
x: He coined it in 1933 as a Cambridge student.

s: On which date did the Muslim League observe Direct Action Day?
x: Direct Action Day was 16 August 1946, called for Pakistan; it led to the Calcutta killings.

s: In which city did Direct Action Day (1946) lead to large-scale killings?
x: Direct Action Day saw the Calcutta killings.

s: The word 'Pakistan' was coined in which pamphlet?
o: Pakistan or the Partition of India
x: Rahmat Ali coined the word 'Pakistan' in the pamphlet Now or Never.

s: Who wrote 'Pakistan or the Partition of India'?
x: B.R. Ambedkar wrote Pakistan or the Partition of India; Rahmat Ali wrote Now or Never and Rafiq Zakaria wrote The Man Who Divided India.

s: From which book does the quotation on Muslims as the 'greatest bulwark of British power' come?
o: Pakistan or the Partition of India
x: W.W. Hunter wrote it in The Indian Musalmans (1871).

s: Who is the author of 'The Man Who Divided India'?
x: 'The Man Who Divided India' is a book by Rafiq Zakaria. Ambedkar wrote 'Pakistan or the Partition of India'.

s: What did the Muslim League's mass-contact campaigns allege the Congress ministries were establishing?
x: The League's campaigns alleged that Muslims were being subjected to 'Hindu Raj' under the Congress ministries.

s: What did the Muslim League celebrate by observing 'Deliverance Day' on 22 December 1939?
o: The adoption of the Lahore Resolution
The resignation of the Congress provincial ministries
The announcement of the Communal Award
The publication of the Pirpur Report
x: Deliverance Day ('Day of Deliverance and Thanksgiving'), 22 December 1939, celebrated the resignation of the Congress ministries. The Lahore Resolution came in March 1940, the Communal Award in 1932 and the Pirpur Report in 1938.

s: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: Muslim Sufferings under Congress Rule — Fazlul Huq
Pirpur Report — Raja Syed Mohammad Mehdi of Pirpur
x: Fazlul Huq authored Muslim Sufferings under Congress Rule. The Pirpur Report was authored by Raja Syed Mohammad Mehdi of Pirpur.

s: Who prepared the Pirpur Report of 1938?
o: Raja Syed Mohammad Mehdi of Pirpur
x: The Pirpur Report (1938) was by Raja Syed Mohammad Mehdi of Pirpur; Sharif wrote the 1939 Bihar report.

s: Who wrote 'Muslim Sufferings under Congress Rule' (December 1939)?
x: Fazlul Huq wrote it in December 1939, after the Pirpur (1938) and Sharif (1939) reports.

s: Who gave the slogan 'Divide and Quit'?
x: During the Second World War Jinnah asked the British to 'Divide and Quit': divide India into Hindustan and Pakistan and then leave. 'Quit India' was Gandhi's call.

s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
x: The RSS was founded in 1925 at Nagpur by K.B. Hedgewar. The other pairs incorrectly interchange the dates, places or persons associated with the two organisations.

s: Where was the Hindu Mahasabha founded in 1915?
x: It was founded at Haridwar during the Kumbh Mela in 1915; the RSS was founded at Nagpur.

s: Who founded the Hindu Mahasabha?
x: Madan Mohan Malaviya founded it; it was first called Sarvadeshik Hindu Sabha and renamed in 1921.

s: Where did Hedgewar found the RSS in 1925?
x: The RSS was founded on 27 September 1925 at Nagpur.

s: By what name was the Hindu Mahasabha first known before it was renamed in 1921?
x: Founded in 1915 at Haridwar by Malaviya, it was first called the Sarvadeshik Hindu Sabha and renamed in 1921.

s: Who was elected president of the Hindu Mahasabha in 1937 and presided over its Ahmedabad session?
x: V.D. Savarkar was elected president of the Hindu Mahasabha in 1937 (Ahmedabad session) and held the post till 1943.

s: What did separate electorates do that made them the seed of the Two-Nation Theory?
x: Separate electorates institutionalised religion in representation, sowing the seed of the Two-Nation Theory.

s: Along with separate electorates, what did the Lucknow Pact of 1916 accept?
o: Universal adult franchise and linguistic provinces
Complete independence and abolition of legislatures
Reserved seats only for depressed classes in joint electorates
Weightage and a communal veto based on a three-fourths rule
x: The Lucknow Pact accepted separate electorates, weightage and a communal veto requiring a three-fourths rule.

s: The Government of India Act, 1935 gave Muslims what share of seats in the Federal Legislature?
x: The 1935 Act gave Muslims 33% of the seats in the Federal Legislature, extending separate electorates further.

s: What was the principal change introduced by the Poona Pact in relation to the Communal Award?
o: The Muslim League was given a communal veto
Separate electorates for Muslims were abolished
Reserved seats in joint electorates replaced separate electorates for the depressed classes
Separate electorates were extended to all Europeans
x: The Poona Pact replaced separate electorates for the depressed classes with reserved seats in joint electorates.

s: What was the long-term political consequence of the Indian Councils Act, 1909?
o: It abolished communal representation in legislatures.
It legally institutionalised communalism and contributed to the growth of the Two-Nation Theory.
It established complete responsible government at the Centre.
It introduced universal adult franchise in British India.
x: The 1909 Act legally institutionalised communal representation, thereby strengthening communal politics and contributing to the emergence of the Two-Nation Theory.

s: Which one of the following Acts first introduced separate (communal) electorates for Muslims in British India?
x: The Indian Councils Act, 1909 (Morley-Minto Reforms) introduced separate electorates for Muslims, with weightage; Minto is called the Father of Communal Electorate. The 1892 Act did not create them; the 1919 Act extended them to Sikhs, Indian Christians, Anglo-Indians and Europeans; the 1935 Act extended them further to depressed classes, women and labour.

s: Who is called the 'Father of Communal Electorate'?
x: Lord Minto is called the Father of Communal Electorate, after the 1909 Morley-Minto Reforms.

s: To which groups did the Government of India Act, 1919 extend separate electorates?
o: Sikhs, Indian Christians, Anglo-Indians and Europeans
x: The 1919 Act extended them to Sikhs, Indian Christians, Anglo-Indians and Europeans; the 1932 Award and 1935 Act extended them further.

s: By which of the following were separate electorates extended to the depressed classes?
x: The Communal Award (1932) extended them to the depressed classes; the Poona Pact replaced it with reserved seats.

s: Which of the following statements about Indian Opinion is INCORRECT?
o: Its first issue appeared in June 1904.
It was Gandhi's paper in South Africa.
It was printed in English, Gujarati, Hindi and Tamil.
Mansukhlal Hiralal Nazar was its first editor.
x: Indian Opinion first appeared in June 1903, not June 1904.

s: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
x: Harijan was a weekly started in 1933; it was not a Gujarati monthly started in 1919. Young India was an English weekly, while Navajivan was a Gujarati journal.

s: Who edited the newspaper Swadeshabhimani?
x: Swadeshabhimani was edited by Ramakrishna Pillai. Vande Matram was Aurobindo's English paper; Harijan Bandhu and Harijan Sewak were Gandhi's Gujarati and Hindi papers.

s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Comrade – Jawaharlal Nehru and Rafi Ahmed Kidwai
x: Mook Nayak was Ambedkar's paper; Young India was Gandhi's, Comrade Muhammad Ali's, and Qaumi Awaz was linked with Nehru and Rafi Ahmed Kidwai.

s: With whom are the journals Indian Opinion, Navajivan and Harijan associated?
x: Indian Opinion, Navajivan and Harijan are associated with Gandhi's journalistic work.

s: In which language was Young India, edited by Gandhi from 1919, published?
x: Young India was an English weekly.

s: Gandhi's Anasakti Yoga is a Gujarati rendering, with commentary, of which text?
x: Anasakti Yoga is Gandhi's Gujarati rendering of the Gita with commentary.

s: How many volumes do the Collected Works of Mahatma Gandhi in English run to?
x: The Collected Works run to 100 volumes, published by the Publications Division.

s: In which journal was Gandhi's autobiography first serialised?
x: Navajivan was Gandhi's Gujarati paper in which his autobiography was serialised.

s: Which one of the following works was written in Gujarati?
o: The Story of My Experiments with Truth
x: The Story of My Experiments with Truth was written in Gujarati. Songs from Prison consisted of English translations, while Young India was an English weekly.

s: With whom was the Urdu journal Al-Hilal associated?
x: Al-Hilal was Abul Kalam Azad's Urdu journal; Young India, Navajivan and Indian Opinion were Gandhi's.

s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Gandhi started Indian Opinion in South Africa in 1903.
2. Mansukhlal Hiralal Nazar was the first editor of Indian Opinion.
Which of the above statements is/are correct?
x: Both are correct: Gandhi started Indian Opinion in South Africa in 1903, and Mansukhlal Hiralal Nazar was its first editor.

s: What kind of paper was Harijan, started by Gandhi in 1933?
x: Harijan was a 1933 English weekly; Harijan Bandhu was Gujarati and Harijan Sevak Hindi.

s: Which pair of paper and person is correctly matched?
x: Mook Nayak was Ambedkar's paper; Comrade was Muhammad Ali's and Vande Mataram Aurobindo's.

s: In which prison did Gandhi make the English translations published as 'Songs from Prison' (1930)?
x: Songs from Prison, English versions of Sanskrit hymns and Upanishadic lyrics, was made in Yerawada Prison.

s: In which language was Harijan Bandhu, started by Gandhi in 1933, published?
x: Harijan was in English, Harijan Bandhu in Gujarati and Harijan Sevak in Hindi.

s:
Match the following:
List-I (Paper)
A. Harijan
B. Harijan Bandhu
C. Harijan Sevak
List-II (Language)
1. Hindi
2. English
3. Gujarati
Select the correct answer using the code given below:
x: All three began in 1933: Harijan in English, Harijan Bandhu in Gujarati, Harijan Sevak in Hindi.

s: Which body published the Collected Works of Mahatma Gandhi?
x: The Collected Works of Mahatma Gandhi (100 volumes in English) were brought out by the Publications Division.

s: Who among the following were associated with the paper Yugantar?
o: Aurobindo Ghosh and Bipin Chandra Pal
Bhupendra Nath Dutt and Barindra Kumar Ghosh
Bal Gangadhar Tilak and G.G. Agarkar
x: Yugantar was the paper of Bhupendra Nath Dutt and Barindra Kumar Ghosh, not of Gandhi; Indian Mirror was of Manmohan Ghosh and Debendranath Tagore.

s: Why is Pravasi Bharatiya Divas observed on 9 January?
o: Gandhi founded the Natal Indian Congress
Gandhi returned to India from South Africa, landing at Bombay
x: Gandhi returned from South Africa and landed at Bombay on 9 January 1915, the date now observed as Pravasi Bharatiya Divas. The Natal Indian Congress dates to 1894, Champaran to 1917, and Kochrab Ashram was set up later in 1915.

s: Who advised Gandhi, on his return in 1915, to spend a year observing India before starting any movement?
x: His political guru Gopal Krishna Gokhale advised him to spend a year observing India first.

s: Which one of the following correctly associates the early Indian satyagrahas with their principal issues?
x: Champaran concerned indigo, Ahmedabad concerned mill wages, and Kheda concerned remission of land revenue.

s: Where did Gandhi land on his return to India on 9 January 1915?
x: Gandhi landed at Bombay on 9 January 1915.

s: For which of the following did Gandhi receive the Kaisar-i-Hind gold medal in 1915?
o: Recruitment drive in the First World War
x: The Kaisar-i-Hind gold medal (1915) was given for his ambulance work in South Africa.

s: During which struggle did Gandhi undertake his first hunger strike in India?
x: Ahmedabad 1918 (mill wages) was the first hunger strike; Champaran was civil disobedience and Kheda non-cooperation.

s: Gandhi read Unto This Last during a train journey in 1904. What did he do soon afterwards?
x: After reading Unto This Last in 1904, Gandhi founded the Phoenix Settlement soon afterwards.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about Gandhi's settlements and ashrams?
o: Sabarmati Ashram was established before Tolstoy Farm
x: Sabarmati Ashram came in 1917, after Tolstoy Farm (1910); the order is Phoenix (1904), Tolstoy Farm (1910), Sabarmati (1917), Sevagram (1936).

s: Which Andhra leader worked at Gandhi's Sabarmati Satyagraha Ashram?
x: Potti Sriramulu worked at the Sabarmati Satyagraha Ashram.

s: With whose help did Gandhi set up Tolstoy Farm near Johannesburg?
x: Tolstoy Farm (1910) was set up with Hermann Kallenbach as a cooperative settlement for satyagrahis and their families.

s: Which was Gandhi's first ashram in India?
x: Kochrab Ashram, Ahmedabad (1915) was his first ashram in India; Sabarmati followed in 1917.

s:
Consider the following statements about Tolstoy Farm:
1. It was set up near Johannesburg in 1910.
2. The Indian National Congress helped to found it.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: Tolstoy Farm was set up near Johannesburg in 1910; the INC had no role in it.

s: Where is the Sadaqat Ashram, associated with Gandhi's work in Bihar?
x: Sadaqat Ashram is at Patna and was linked with Gandhi's work in Bihar.

s: Which jail did Gandhi call his 'Mandir'?
x: Gandhi called Yerawada Jail his 'Mandir' (temple).

s: Where was Mahatma Gandhi born on 2 October 1869?
x: Gandhi was born at Porbandar; Rajkot was where he later practised and Bhavnagar is where he studied at Samaldas College.

s: In which year did Gandhi go to South Africa for Dada Abdullah's case?
x: After his practice in Rajkot and Bombay did not succeed, Gandhi went to South Africa in 1893 for Dada Abdullah's case.

s: At which Inn of Court in London did Gandhi train as a barrister?
x: Gandhi trained as a barrister at the Inner Temple in London.

s: Before going to London, Gandhi studied at which college?
x: Gandhi studied at Samaldas College, Bhavnagar, before studying law at the Inner Temple, London.

s: During which years did Gandhi study law in London?
x: Gandhi studied law at the Inner Temple, London, from 1888 to 1891.

s: Where did Gandhi set up his unsuccessful legal practice after returning from London?
x: His legal practice at Rajkot and Bombay did not succeed; in 1893 he went to South Africa.

s: In which year did Gandhi undergo his first jail term in South Africa?
x: Gandhi's first jail term was in 1908, after the burning of registration certificates; 1913 was the year of the Great March.

s: What happened to Gandhi at Pietermaritzburg station on 7 June 1893?
o: He formed the Natal Indian Congress.
He was arrested for burning registration certificates.
He was thrown out of a first-class railway compartment.
He delivered his first public speech in South Africa.
x: On 7 June 1893, Gandhi was thrown out of a first-class compartment at Pietermaritzburg station.

s: The first satyagraha in South Africa in 1906 was launched against which measure?
o: The Asiatic Registration Ordinance, known as the Black Act
x: The first South African satyagraha in 1906 opposed the Asiatic Registration Ordinance, called the Black Act, in the Transvaal.

s: Which Act of 1914 abolished the £3 poll tax and recognised Indian marriages in South Africa?
x: The Indian Relief Act of 1914, which followed the Great March of 1913, both abolished the poll tax and recognised Indian marriages.

s: Which country is regarded as the 'laboratory' where Gandhi developed satyagraha in 1906?
x: Gandhi developed and experimented with satyagraha in South Africa in 1906, which is why South Africa is called its laboratory.

s: In which year did Gandhi found the Natal Indian Congress?
x: Gandhi founded the Natal Indian Congress in 1894.

s: Against which of the following was the Great March of 1913 in South Africa mainly directed?
x: The 1913 Great March opposed the £3 poll tax and the invalidation of Indian marriages; miners and indentured workers joined.

s: In South Africa, Gandhi worked as a compounder in which hospital as part of his 'Seva Dharma'?
x: He adopted Seva Dharma by working as a compounder in Rustomji's charity hospital and serving the Boer War wounded.

s: For about how many years did Gandhi stay in South Africa?
x: Gandhi was in South Africa from 1893 to 1914, about 21 years.

s: In which year did Gandhi return his Kaisar-i-Hind gold medal?
x: Gandhi returned the medal (awarded in 1915 for his South African ambulance work) in 1920 during the Khilafat and Non-Cooperation campaign.

s: Who called Gandhi a 'half-naked fakir' in 1931?
x: Winston Churchill, not Lord Irwin, called Gandhi a 'half-naked fakir' in 1931.

s: Who gave Gandhi the title 'Mahatma'?
x: Rabindranath Tagore called Gandhi 'Mahatma' in 1914.

s: In which year did Subhas Chandra Bose call Gandhi 'Father of the Nation'?
x: Bose called Gandhi Father of the Nation on Azad Hind radio, Singapore, on 6 July 1944.

s: In connection with which movement did Gandhi return the Kaisar-i-Hind gold medal in 1920?
x: He returned the medal in 1920 during the Khilafat and Non-Cooperation Movement.

s: From where did Subhas Chandra Bose call Gandhi the 'Father of the Nation' on 6 July 1944?
x: Bose called Gandhi 'Father of the Nation' in a broadcast on Azad Hind Radio from Singapore on 6 July 1944.

s: How does Gandhi's Hind Swaraj present swaraj?
x: Hind Swaraj presents swaraj as self-rule and advocates self-reliance and rural life, while critiquing industrialisation.

s: Which government banned Hind Swaraj in 1910?
x: Hind Swaraj was banned by the Bombay Government in 1910.

s: Aboard which ship did Gandhi write Hind Swaraj?
x: Hind Swaraj was written in 1909 aboard the Kildonan Castle, from London to South Africa.

s: Who translated Hind Swaraj into English?
x: Gandhi translated Hind Swaraj into English himself, to get round the ban.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about Hind Swaraj?
x: Hind Swaraj was against industrialisation and modern civilisation, stressing self-reliance and rural life.

s: Who is the author of 'Hind Swaraj'?
x: 'Hind Swaraj' was written by Gandhi and sets out his idea of Swaraj.

s: Which of the following is associated with the Bhagavad Gita in Gandhi’s system of influences?
o: Passive resistance to the Asiatic Registration Ordinance
The right to break unjust laws
x: Gandhi associated the Bhagavad Gita with Nishkama karma, or action without attachment to the fruits of action.

s: Which of the following are the five Jain vows that influenced Gandhian thought?
o: ahimsa, satya, asteya, aparigraha and swadeshi
ahimsa, satya, asteya, aparigraha and brahmacharya
satya, ahimsa, swaraj, sarvodaya and aparigraha
ahimsa, satya, dana, tapas and brahmacharya
x: The five vows are ahimsa, satya, asteya, aparigraha and brahmacharya; the first four are linked with Parshvanatha and brahmacharya was added by Mahavira.

s: Which work inspired Gandhi's ideas of the dignity of labour and Sarvodaya?
o: Tolstoy's The Kingdom of God Is Within You
x: John Ruskin's Unto This Last inspired Gandhi's ideas of the dignity of labour and Sarvodaya; Thoreau's Civil Disobedience gave him the right to break unjust laws.

s: From whom did Gandhi take the idea of the right to break unjust laws?
x: Thoreau's Civil Disobedience gave Gandhi the right to break unjust laws.

s: Who gave Gandhi a copy of Unto This Last in 1904?
x: Henry Polak gave Gandhi Unto This Last in 1904; it influenced him most.

s: Among the five Jain vows that influenced Gandhi, which was added by Mahavira?
x: The first four vows come from Parshvanatha; brahmacharya was added by Mahavira.

s: Which pair of book and author, as an influence on Gandhi, is INCORRECTLY matched?
o: The Kingdom of God is Within You – John Ruskin
x: The Kingdom of God is Within You was written by Leo Tolstoy, not Ruskin.

s: What was the early English name for 'Satyagraha'?
x: Satyagraha, born in 1906 in the Transvaal, was early rendered in English as 'passive resistance'.

s: Of which of the following was the Rowlatt Satyagraha of 1919 Gandhi's first?
x: The Rowlatt Satyagraha (1919) was Gandhi's first all-India mass movement; Champaran was his first civil disobedience, Ahmedabad his first hunger strike and Kheda his first non-cooperation.

s: Which one of the following is inconsistent with the rules prescribed for a Satyagrahi?
o: Insulting the opponent to expose injustice
x: A Satyagrahi must never insult the opponent. The rules require non-retaliation, submission to arrest and observance of jail discipline.

s: Which one of the following correctly matches the struggle with its distinctive description?
o: Rowlatt Satyagraha — first civil disobedience by Gandhi in India
x: Kheda (1918) is classed as Gandhi's first non-cooperation. The other pairs are wrong: Champaran (1917) was the first civil disobedience, not non-cooperation; Ahmedabad (1918) was the first hunger strike, not an all-India strike; the Rowlatt Satyagraha (1919, hartal) was the first all-India mass movement, not the first civil disobedience.

s: According to Gandhi, which was the first step of satyagraha?
x:
The printed options did not include the correct answer (None of these); it is added as option 5.
No option is the first step. Gandhi called fasting the last weapon of satyagraha ('Fasting unto death is the last and the most potent weapon in the armoury of Satyagraha', Harijan 1946), so 'fasting = first step' is wrong. Strike, picketing and hartal are not named as the first step either.

s: According to Gandhi, what is the driving force of satyagraha?
x: Suffering is the driving force of satyagraha; its aim is not to defeat the enemy.

s: Which form of satyagraha marked the Rowlatt Satyagraha of 1919?
x: The Rowlatt Satyagraha of 1919 used hartal and was the first all-India mass movement.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about satyagraha?
o: Its aim is to defeat the enemy
It was born in 1906 in the Transvaal
x: The aim of satyagraha is not to defeat the enemy; suffering is its driving force.

s: When the only choice was between cowardice and violence, what did Gandhi say he would prefer?
x: Gandhi preferred violence to cowardice when those were the only alternatives; for him ahimsa was a quality of the strong, not of the weak.

s: Which statement correctly distinguishes Gandhi's formulations ‘God is Truth’ and ‘Truth is God’?
o: ‘Truth is God’ was the earlier formulation and ‘God is Truth’ the later one.
‘God is Truth’ was the earlier formulation, while ‘Truth is God’ was the later formulation.
Gandhi rejected both formulations as incompatible.
Both expressions referred only to political freedom.
x: Gandhi initially used the formulation ‘God is Truth’ and later expressed the idea as ‘Truth is God’, giving truth an independent and central status.

s: According to Gandhi, ahimsa is a quality of whom?
x: Gandhi held ahimsa, in thought, word and deed, to be a quality of the brave, not the weak.

s: How is truth described in Gandhian thought?
x: Gandhi described truth as reality: existence, consciousness and bliss.

s:
Consider the following statements about Gandhi's truth and ahimsa:
1. Truth is the end and non-violence the means.
2. 'Truth is God' was his earlier formulation.
3. Ahimsa is to be practised in thought, word and deed.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
x: 'God is Truth' came first and 'Truth is God' later, so statement 2 is wrong.

s: What did Gandhi call politics bereft of religion?
x: Gandhi said politics bereft of religion (meaning morality based on truth and non-violence) is a death-trap.

s: Whose face does Gandhi's Talisman ask a person to recall before taking a step?
x: Gandhi's Talisman requires one to consider the poorest and weakest person before taking a step.

s: According to Gandhi, in what does real swaraj lie?
x: Gandhi said real swaraj is the capacity of all to resist authority when it is abused.

s: What was the key suggestion of Gandhi's politics for governance?
x: Gandhi's politics proposed decentralisation through village panchayats, with no place for authority.

s: How does Gandhi complete the saying 'Means are after all everything'?
o: As the means so the end
x: Gandhi said, 'Means are after all everything. As the means so the end.'

s: Why is Gandhi's concept of Swaraj wider than political independence?
o: self-rule, self-control and the capacity of the masses to govern themselves without coercion
freedom only from foreign economic competition
centralised rule by a single national authority
rule by a hereditary political class
x: For Gandhi, Swaraj meant not merely political freedom but also self-rule, self-control and the ability of people to govern themselves without coercion.

s: Which one of the following is NOT one of the interrelated principles included in Gandhi's concept of Swaraj?
x: Swadeshi, ahimsa, Satyagraha, decentralisation and education for all are included among the interrelated principles of Swaraj. Class dictatorship is not a Gandhian principle.

s: Which of the following is included in Gandhi's concept of Swaraj?
x: Swaraj meant self-rule and self-control, not only political freedom.

s: Who was the Jain thinker who influenced Gandhi?
x: Gandhi was influenced by Jainism in Gujarat, notably by the Jain thinker Raychandbhai.

s: For Gandhi, where did the essence of Christ's teaching lie?
x: Gandhi saw the Sermon on the Mount as the essence of Christ's teaching.

s: Which pair of influence and work is correctly matched?
o: Ruskin – The Kingdom of God is Within You
x: Thoreau wrote Civil Disobedience; Ruskin wrote Unto This Last and Tolstoy The Kingdom of God is Within You.

s: 'Trusteeship' as the basis of property relations is a concept of which school of thought?
x: Trusteeship is Gandhian; Marxism seeks the abolition of private property.

s: Because of which ideal is Gandhi called a philosophical anarchist?
x: His ideal of 'enlightened anarchy' and his view of the State as violence in concentrated form make Gandhi a philosophical anarchist.

s: How is the socialism in the Indian Preamble generally understood?
o: Marxism and Gandhism, with a Marxist inclination
liberalism and Fabianism, with a liberal inclination
capitalism and Marxism, with a capitalist inclination
Marxism and Gandhism, with a Gandhian inclination
x: Indian socialism is described as combining Marxist and Gandhian elements while leaning towards Gandhian socialism.

s: How did Gandhi describe the State?
o: The march of God on earth
x: Gandhi, a philosophical anarchist, called the State violence in concentrated form.

s: Unlike Marxism, what is the method of Gandhism?
x: Gandhism relies on non-violence and change of heart; Marxism on class struggle and revolution.

s: Which of the following is NOT Gandhian?
x: Class dictatorship is not Gandhian; trusteeship, Sarvodaya and means-ends purity are his core values.

s: With which of the following was Vinoba Bhave associated?
x: Vinoba Bhave led the Sarvodaya Samaj; Agnihotri founded the Dev Samaj and Phule the Satyashodhak Samaj.

s: The term 'Sarvodaya' signifies which of the following?
o: Welfare or uplift of all, including the last person
Exclusive economic development of rural areas
x: Sarvodaya means the welfare, uplift or progress of all, with attention reaching the last person.

s: Why did Dr. B.R. Ambedkar criticise the Gandhian village ideal?
o: A seat of caste domination and localism
A unit without any social organisation
x: Ambedkar viewed the village as a seat of caste domination and described it as a sink of localism, ignorance and communalism. He preferred the individual as the basic unit.

s: Who wrote *Sarvodaya Ganam* and translated Gandhi's autobiography into Telugu?
x: Tummala Sitaramamurthy wrote *Sarvodaya Ganam*, inspired by Vinoba, and translated Gandhi's autobiography into Telugu.

s: Who drafted the 'Gandhian Plan'?
x: Shriman Narayan Aggarwal drafted the Gandhian Plan; JP drafted the Sarvodaya Plan.

s: Who wrote the Gandhian Constitution for Free India (1946)?
x: Shriman Narayan Aggarwal wrote it in 1946, with Gandhi's foreword.

s: On which day is Sarvodaya Day observed?
x: Sarvodaya Day is observed on 30 January.

s: Under Bhoodan, what minimum share of their land were landlords asked to gift?
x: Vinoba asked landlords to gift at least one-sixth of their land.

s: Who organised the Sarvodaya Samaj?
x: Vinoba Bhave made Sarvodaya the cornerstone and organised the Sarvodaya Samaj.

s: Who received the first land gift of the Bhoodan movement at Pochampalli on 18 April 1951?
x: Vinoba Bhave began the Bhoodan movement at Pochampalli, receiving the first land gift on 18 April 1951.

s: Who coined the term 'Gandhian Innovation'?
x: Gandhian Innovation (more from less for more people) was coined by Prof. Prahlad and R.A. Mashelkar.

s: How did Gandhi define 'Ramarajya'?
o: Rule by a strong centralised State
Sovereignty of the people based on pure moral authority
Rule of the propertied classes as trustees
x: Gandhi wrote in Harijan (1937) that Ramarajya meant sovereignty of the people based on pure moral authority; he said it did not mean Hindu Raj.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the Gandhian economic approach?
o: It directs production primarily toward profit maximisation
x: Gandhi wanted production directed toward need, not profit; a non-violent economy needs decentralisation and self-reliance.

s: According to Gandhi, by what should a country's economy be defined?
o: Climate, land and the nature of its citizens
x: Gandhi held each economy should fit its climate, land and the nature of its citizens.

s:
Consider the following statements about the Gandhian economy:
1. Production should be for need (consumption), not for profit.
2. Heavy industry should get priority over agriculture and village industries.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: Gandhi wanted production for need and gave priority to agriculture and village and cottage industries over heavy industry.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about Gandhian trusteeship?
o: It sought class harmony rather than class struggle.
It was applied only to zamindars and not to capitalists.
Its roots lay in the Gita's idea of non-possession and the English law of trusts.
It was applied to mill owners such as those of Ahmedabad.
x: Trusteeship was applied to both capitalists and zamindars (e.g. the Ahmedabad mill owners), not only to zamindars.

s: With which place and year is Gandhi's idea of trusteeship linked?
x: Trusteeship is linked to South Africa, 1903, when he had a law firm at Johannesburg.

s: With what wage rise did the Ahmedabad Mill Strike of 1918 end?
x: Gandhi's fast in the 1918 Ahmedabad Mill Strike won a 35% wage rise.

s: Who drafted the 'Practical Trusteeship Formula'?
x: Narhari Parikh and Kishorelal Mashruwala drafted it while Gandhi was held at Aga Khan Palace; M.L. Dantwala refined it.

s:
Consider the following statements about Gandhian trusteeship:
1. It applied to both capitalists and zamindars.
2. The Textile Labour Association of 1920 used arbitration.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: Trusteeship covered capitalists and zamindars, and the Textile Labour Association (1920) used arbitration and non-violence.

s: Which of the following did the 'Practical Trusteeship Formula' propose?
o: A minimum living wage and a ceiling on income
x: The formula drafted by Narhari Parikh and Kishorelal Mashruwala proposed a minimum living wage and a ceiling on income.

s: Which of the following was an aim of swadeshi and khadi?
x: Swadeshi and khadi promoted rural employment, self-reliance and a bridge between towns and villages. Gandhi popularised the charkha and khadi for these purposes.

s: Which organisations were established in 1925 and 1934 respectively?
o: All India Village Industries Association and All India Spinners' Association
All India Spinners' Association and All India Village Industries Association
Textile Labour Association and All India Spinners' Association
All India Spinners' Association and Constructive Programme Committee
x: The All India Spinners' Association was established in 1925, while the All India Village Industries Association was established in 1934.

s: Which place in Andhra Pradesh is noted for producing the finest khadi in India?
x: Ponduru in Srikakulam district is noted for the finest khadi in India; Guravareddypalem is linked with Prakasam's Khadi Development Centre.

s: Where was Prakasam's Khadi Development Centre that got Rs 10,000 from the AISA?
x: The centre at Guravareddypalem (Guntur) got Rs 10,000 from the All India Spinners' Association.

s: Which pair of body and year is INCORRECTLY matched?
x: The All India Village Industries Association dates from 1934; 1925 is the Spinners' Association.

s: Which one of the following pairs of a Gandhian Directive Principle and its Article is correctly matched?
x: Article 43 promotes cottage industries. Article 40 deals with village panchayats and Article 47 with prohibition of intoxicating drinks, so the other pairs interchange the Articles.

s: Which of the following was NOT an item of Gandhi's constructive programme?
x: Constructive programme items included khadi, prohibition, removal of untouchability, national schools, Hindu-Muslim unity and village panchayats.

s: Which Article of the Constitution directs the State to promote cottage industries?
x: Article 43 covers cottage industries; 40 panchayats and 47 prohibition.

s: What was Gandhi's approach to rural development called?
x: Gandhi's approach to rural development was Samagra Gramseva, an all-round service of the village.

s: Which Article of the Constitution directs the State to organise village panchayats?
x: Article 40, a Directive Principle, asks the State to organise village panchayats as units of self-government, a Gandhian ideal.

s: Which one of the following correctly represents Gandhi’s stated influence from The Kingdom of God is Within You?
o: The right to break unjust laws
x: Gandhi took the ideas of love and non-violence from Leo Tolstoy’s The Kingdom of God is Within You.

s: Which of the following pairs relating to Gandhi's ideas is INCORRECTLY matched?
o: Term 'bread labour' – T.M. Bondaref, via Tolstoy
Bread labour – the Gita's idea of yajna
Right to break unjust laws – Thoreau's Civil Disobedience
x: The sources of bread labour were Tolstoy (from Bondaref) and Ruskin's Unto This Last, linked by Gandhi to yajna; Thoreau's work gave the right to break unjust laws.

s: In which year did Gandhi's Gujarati retelling of Unto This Last, titled 'Sarvodaya', appear?
x: Gandhi's Gujarati retelling 'Sarvodaya' of Ruskin's Unto This Last appeared in 1908.

s: In which year was Gandhi's booklet Constructive Programme published?
x: Constructive Programme was a 1941 booklet by Gandhi.

s: From whom did Tolstoy take the term 'bread labour'?
x: Tolstoy took the term bread labour from T.M. Bondaref; Gandhi drew it from Tolstoy and Ruskin.

s: To which concept of the Gita did Gandhi link the idea of bread labour?
x: Gandhi linked bread labour to the Gita's yajna.

s: From which of the following did Gandhi NOT draw his idea of bread labour?
x: Thoreau gave civil disobedience, not bread labour.

s: Which of the following represents Gandhi's route for the uplift of communities subjected to untouchability?
o: Separate electorates, political boycott and armed resistance
Exclusive reliance on litigation and legislative vetoes
Moral persuasion, temple entry, funds, schools and hostels, and constructive work
Economic isolation of orthodox Hindu groups
x: Gandhi's approach combined moral persuasion, temple entry, funds, schools and hostels, and constructive work.

s: How did Gandhi describe untouchability?
o: A matter for the State alone
x: Gandhi called untouchability 'a blot on Hinduism' and sought reform from within Hindu society.

s: Which term used by Gandhi was rejected by Ambedkar and Dalit leaders, who criticised caste-Hindu paternalism?
x: Ambedkar and Dalit leaders rejected the term 'Harijan' and criticised what they saw as caste-Hindu paternalism.

s: From whom was the term 'Harijan', meaning 'children of God', taken?
x: Gandhi adopted the term ‘Harijan’, meaning ‘children of God’, from the Gujarati saint Narsi Mehta.

s: How did Gandhi want untouchability to be removed?
x: Gandhi called untouchability a blot on Hinduism and sought reform from within Hindu society.

s: What did the Congress ministries formed after 1937 provide to Harijans?
x: The Congress ministries of 1937 gave free education to Harijans.

s: Which of the following was NOT among the activities associated with the Harijan Sevak Sangh?
o: Introducing separate electorates for the Depressed Classes
Promoting entry into wells and temples
x: The Sangh worked for access to wells, schools and temples, and promoted schools, hostels, cooperatives, inter-dining and inter-caste marriage. Separate electorates were a political demand associated with the Poona Pact debate, not its activity.

s: Who served as secretary of the Harijan Sevak Sangh?
x: Thakkar Bapa was the secretary; G.D. Birla was its first president.

s: On which date did Gandhi found the Harijan Sevak Sangh, while in prison?
x: The Sangh was founded on 30 September 1932, after the Poona Pact.

s: Who was the first president of the Harijan Sevak Sangh?
x: G.D. Birla was the first president of the Harijan Sevak Sangh; Amritlal Thakkar (Thakkar Bapa) was its secretary.

s: What was the earlier name of the Harijan Sevak Sangh?
x: The Harijan Sevak Sangh, founded by Gandhi in 1932, was first called the All India Anti-Untouchability League.

s: After which of the following did Gandhi found the Harijan Sevak Sangh in 1932?
x: Gandhi founded the Harijan Sevak Sangh on 30 September 1932, soon after the Poona Pact with Ambedkar.

s: Which of the following correctly describes Gandhi's Harijan tour?
o: November 1933 to July 1934, covering about 20,000 km from Wardha Ashram
August 1934 to March 1935, covering about 10,000 km from Sabarmati
January 1933 to December 1933, covering about 5,000 km from Poona
November 1932 to July 1933, covering about 20,000 km from Mumbai
x: Gandhi's Harijan tour ran from November 1933 to July 1934, covered about 20,000 km, began from the Wardha Ashram and collected funds for the Harijan Sevak Sangh. Orthodox groups disrupted some meetings.

s: Gandhi's weekly 'Harijan' was started in which year, with its first issue brought out from which place?
x: Harijan weekly brought out its first issue on 11 February 1933 at Poona. 1919 is when Gandhi began editing Young India; 1903 at Durban is Indian Opinion; 1936 is the founding of Sevagram at Wardha.

s: About how much distance did Gandhi's Harijan tour of November 1933 – July 1934 cover?
x: The Harijan tour covered about 20,000 km and raised funds for the Sangh.

s: From where did Gandhi begin his Harijan tour of 1933-34?
x: The Harijan tour started from Wardha Ashram in November 1933.

s: What was the main aim of Nai Talim, or Basic Education?
o: Replacing manual work with purely literary education
Providing higher education exclusively in English
Training students only for government employment
Making villages self-sufficient through vocational and craft-centred education
x: Gandhi's Basic Education was vocational and craft-centred, sought to make villages self-sufficient and aimed to dignify manual labour.

s: Which of the following pairs relating to the Wardha Scheme of Basic Education is correctly matched?
o: Duration of free and compulsory education – five years
x: The Wardha Scheme was drawn up by the Zakir Hussain Committee, adopted in 1937 and envisaged seven years of free and compulsory education.

s: For how many years did the Wardha Scheme propose free and compulsory education?
x: Basic education was to be free and compulsory for 7 years, from age 7 to 14.

s: What was to be the medium of instruction under Nai Talim?
x: Nai Talim called for teaching in the mother tongue, with learning through a productive craft.

s: Which committee drew up the Wardha Scheme of Basic Education (1937)?
x: The Wardha Scheme, adopted at the Wardha Educational Conference of 1937, was drawn up by the Zakir Hussain Committee.

s: Who propounded the scheme of Basic Education (Nai Talim)?
x: Basic education (Nai Talim) was propounded by Gandhi and adopted at the Wardha Educational Conference, 1937.

s:
Consider the following statements about Gandhi's views on women:
1. He opposed purdah and child marriage.
2. He opposed dowry.
3. He opposed the remarriage of child widows.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: Gandhi opposed purdah, child marriage and dowry; statement 3 is wrong as he supported the remarriage of child widows.

s: What was Gandhi's stand on the remarriage of child widows?
o: He left it to caste panchayats
x: Gandhi opposed purdah, child marriage and dowry but supported the remarriage of child widows.

s: For Gandhi, what was the bedrock of Indian nationalism?
x: Gandhi regarded Hindu-Muslim unity as the bedrock of nationalism and backed the Khilafat cause for it.

s:
Consider the following statements about Gandhi's religious outlook:
1. Sarva dharma samabhava means equal respect for all religions.
2. His ashram prayers drew on many faiths.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: Both are correct: sarva dharma samabhava is equal respect for all religions, and the ashram prayers drew on many faiths.

s: What does sarva dharma samabhava mean?
o: Separation of religion from all public prayer
The superiority of one religion over all others
Acceptance of only reformist Hindu sects
x: Sarva dharma samabhava means equal respect for all religions. Gandhi's ashram prayers drew upon several faiths.

s: Besides Calcutta, where did Gandhi fast during the communal riots of 1946-47?
x: His riot-time fasts of 1946-47 were at Calcutta and Noakhali, not Vaikom or Guruvayur.

s: Which of the following was NOT a leader of the Vaikom Satyagraha (1924-25)?
x: Vaikom was led by T.K. Madhavan, K. Kelappan and K.P. Kesava Menon; Potti Sriramulu led the Nellore temple-entry fasts of 1946.

s: During the Guruvayur Satyagraha, Gandhi persuaded whom to end his fast in 1932?
x: K. Kelappan led the Guruvayur Satyagraha (1931-32); Gandhi persuaded him to end his fast.

s: Who undertook the temple-entry fasts of 1946 in Nellore?
x: Potti Sriramulu undertook the Nellore temple-entry fasts in 1946.

s: Where did Potti Sriramulu undertake temple-entry fasts in 1946?
x: Potti Sriramulu fasted for temple entry of Harijans at Nellore in 1946.
